Currently deployed services do not live-stream the VV
They just capture/render VV in place and generate 2D replay video
A high-quality frame of the whole scene: >30MB
14.4Gbps@60fps

lists.text:
The sender separates a scene into multiple segments
On the viewer side, predict its field-of-view (FoV) a few frames ahead
Request the segments the predicted FoV intersects with
Pretty much all the state-of-the-art volumetric video research hires this approach
Originally used in 360° video streaming
Requires real-time FoV prediction and low-latency transport

lists.text:
A MoQ track corresponds to a segment
Moqtopus for the publisher/subscriber, MOQtail for the relay
Publisher repeatedly sends 7s of baseball point-cloud VV
Subscriber SUBSCRIBEs the track corresponds to the segment within a predicted FoV (5 frames ahead)
When it’s out of the FoV, unsubscribe it (STOP_SENDING)
The publisher and relay are connected with 100GbE so upstream bandwidth won’t be a bottleneck

lists.text:
My hypothesis was the relay CPU was saturated because of frequent subscription churn and its state management
MOQtail handled subscription churn perfectly
Subscription/unsubscription could happen at every frame in the worst case
I gave MOQtail (or tokio) 10 cores, but it only used 3 cores at maximum
Even when scaling the number of subscribers to 50
The time from SUBSCRIBE reception to the next write_all to the corresponding stream was only few microseconds
It was not the relay causing the frame drop

lists.text:
In recent version of MoQ, Subscriber UNSUBSCRIBEs by sending STOP_SENDING on the bidirectional request stream.
(We don’t UNSUBSCRIBE anymore btw)
Then the relay sends RESET_STREAM to all streams in the subscription, cancelling the stream right away
Objects still in the send queue could be discarded

lists.text:
Forward is a binary parameter in a subscription
REQUEST_UPDATE(forward=0) tells the relay to stop forwarding objects in the subscription
The relay retains the subscription so there’s no stream reset happening
It was originally defined to pre-warm the subscription
Also useful for frequent track switching and prediction like this workload.

lists.text:
Subscriber Priority is per-subscription priority set by a subscriber
Relay decides which object to send next based on the priority
Subscriber Priority takes precedence over Publisher Priority and Group Order
I scored segments in a predicted FoV based on the distance/angle from the predicted position
score = round(7/2(normalized_distance + normalized_angle)) * 32
↑ Basically separates segments into 8 priorities
Closer the higher priority, the closer to the center the higher priority

lists.text:
MOQtail applies Subscriber Priority to QUIC’s stream priority
So QUIC stack (Quinn) can schedule packets in its send queue based on the priority
When Quinn’s write size reaches the flow control limit, write tasks from streams are held on Tokio runtime
`stream.write_all(&object).await`
When the limit is extended or ack’s received, Tokio polls one of the write task of streams
Since Tokio does NOT know about the Subscriber Priority, a write task of the stream with the highest priority does not necessarily get executed first.
I have set a shared write queue in MOQtail, and write in the order of the Subscriber Priority

Send buffer, recv window and maximum number of streams are radically extended
Renderer’s queue is also optimized to wait longer for higher priority objects
Scoring is a design choice (some might want to see everything with lower quality)
